hero.headline: It keeps its own hours, and travels a third as heavy
hero.sub: Two releases in one upgrade. v0.22.0 was built but never reached anyone, so everything it carried arrives here. Your brain can now be given work on a schedule and left alone with it — and when you do sit down together, everything it knows loads in 16,320 characters instead of 48,964. Nothing was dropped. What got cut was repetition.

shot.alt: The Automations page before you own one: the headline "Put the brain on a schedule" over a diagram of three scheduled jobs — a daily digest, a Friday report, a Tuesday research prompt — feeding one dispatcher, which spawns a headless claude session that writes a dated file, sends a notification, and reads and updates a pattern
shot.caption: The whole loop, before you write your first one.

blocks.title: A job is a prompt and a clock
blocks.body:
There is no built-in digest command and no hardcoded job type. What the job IS lives entirely in the prompt you write; the CLI carries only the schedule, the model, the effort and the timeout.

If you can say it, it can run at six every evening.

shot.alt: Three automation cards: End of day digest every day at 18:00 with a last run this afternoon, Dependency drift check on Tuesdays at 09:00, and Friday weekly report at 17:00, each with a Run now button

blocks.title: It gets better at the job
blocks.body:
Something that starts from zero every time repeats its mistakes forever, and nobody is there to watch it happen. So every automation keeps a pattern of its own: a standing playbook, and a short ledger of what it learned.

It reads that before it starts, and adds to it when it finishes. A run that hit a broken endpoint on Sunday knows that next Sunday.

shot.alt: The pattern of a real automation: a playbook the run wrote itself describing the order to gather in, above four dated lessons about which commands work on this vault
shot.caption: Every line here was written by the run itself. None of it by hand.

blocks.title: You can watch the work, not just the result
blocks.body:
The document a run leaves behind is the conclusion with the working thrown away — which is the wrong half the moment it surprises you.

So every run keeps its session. Open it and the whole thing replays: each tool call and what it was given, which ones failed, how long it took and what it cost.

shot.alt: A run's session: 32 tool calls, 2 failed, 33 turns, $1.8097, above the list of Bash calls it made, with two of them marked in red

blocks.title: It runs with nobody watching, so it starts locked

items.title: Nothing runs until you say so
items.text: The whole thing ships switched off. You install the dispatcher yourself, and approve each automation on this machine, before anything fires.

items.title: Approval is a fingerprint of what will happen
items.text: The prompt, the output instructions, the model, the effort, the timeout, where it writes and whether it learns. Change any of them — including a teammate's synced edit — and the job stops until a person looks again.

items.title: It stays on your machine
items.text: A new automation, its history and its output stay off the team's shared brain until you share it. Unsharing stops what happens next; it cannot retrieve what already left.

items.title: The notification says what happened
items.text: Not "a file was written" — the run's own first sentence, titled by the automation, with the document one click away. Success and failure sound different.

blocks.text: The pattern is deliberately outside that fingerprint. It changes on every run, and a job that asked for approval daily would only teach you to approve without reading — so it reaches the model as notes, ordered after the approved prompt, framed as observations that lose to the instructions.

items.label: Characters at session start
items.note: measured on a real mature vault

items.label: Pattern files written
items.note: clustered by rule, not by bullet

blocks.title: The same brain. A third of the weight.
blocks.body:
The session-start preload had been growing faster than the vault it describes, until it needed a compression ladder to fit — which is a way of hiding content that should never have been sent. So the default got denser instead. Features are a name, a status and a path. Knowledge that isn't pinned is an honest count and the command to reach the rest. The warm-knowledge section is simply gone.

It now arrives whole, with no truncation banner, on a vault where it used to be cut in half.

shot.alt: The Core page of a vault: a PEOPLE section with the active person at the top, above the core files — soul, memory, style guide, tech stack, changelog, releases and taxonomy — with the soul document open in the reader beside them
shot.caption: The shape of a brain after 0.23.0: a person, and a constitution-only soul.

blocks.title: It knows who is at the keyboard
blocks.body:
The old user file was one document trying to be a person, a roster and a junk drawer at once. It's gone. Everyone gets their own constitution now, loaded word for word when they're the one working, resolved from your git identity — with nothing about your machine written into the shared brain.

Your existing vault is moved for you. The mechanical half happens on upgrade; the prose that needed judgement is handed to your agent rather than guessed at.

shot.alt: The Core file list: a PEOPLE heading with the active person under it, then CORE FILES listing soul, active-decisions, style-guide, tech-stack, CHANGELOG, RELEASES and taxonomy — with no 1.user.md among them
shot.caption: No user file. A person, then the core files.

blocks.title: A rule can be shortened. It can no longer be silenced.
blocks.body:
A soul holding every conditional rule is a soul nobody reads — and when space got tight, those rules used to collapse into an anonymous folder count. The conditional half now lives in patterns, clustered by the rule it carries.

Patterns get their own block in every snapshot, at every size, under a warning you can't miss.

shot.alt: The Knowledge page with the Patterns folder expanded to 17 entries, showing pattern cards whose descriptions are the rule itself — budget demotion floor prevents blinding, build and propagate order, byte-surgical section editing — each tagged by domain
shot.caption: 17 patterns, each described by the rule it carries.

items.title: Enter reaches the turn that's already running
items.text: A message you send mid-turn is picked up at the next tool boundary, inside the same turn. Holding one for later is now its own button, with the editable row it always had.

items.title: Every conversation is still there
items.text: A searchable picker reopens anything this project has on disk — 372 of them here, cold in half a second. The 119 that were machine-spawned are set aside by default, and one click brings them back.

items.title: A headless run reads as an agent
items.text: Work your agent hands to another Claude now renders as a sub-agent with its own card, not as an anonymous background shell. Its tool calls group under the run that made them.

items.title: A row names the thing, not the type
items.text: The skill, the pattern, the host, the file — with the folder truncated instead of the filename, because the filename was the only part that differed. And a new tab names itself in a moment rather than a minute.

blocks.title: Two new ways to find things
lines: Changelog — page 1/185 (554 matching entries, newest first)
- 2026-07-30 [feat] cli: New dreamcontext changelog list — paginated
- 2026-07-30 [feat] snapshot: Patterns get their own block with a HARD
# recall ranks by relevance. these two answer "what happened, in order".

items.title: Memory arrives whole
items.text: A memory file at or under 4,000 characters is no longer squeezed again at render time. Sleep is memory's compressor; doing it twice was just taxation.

items.title: Tasks are accounted for
items.text: They show their real name, with the slug demoted to an address. Under pressure the list turns into an accounting: detailed, named and counted always add up to the total.

items.title: Nothing is a dead end
items.text: Every inventory ends with how to reach the rest of it — at every size, including the smallest. A shortened section always tells you where the remainder went.

items.title: Turkish names survive
items.text: Accented and Turkish titles fold to ASCII before they're turned into a filename, so "Öğretmen fiyatı" keeps its letters instead of arriving mangled.

blocks.title: And the answers themselves read better

items.title: A long answer is not a wall
items.text: The transcript's leading opened up, and a findings list — the shape most long answers take — no longer sits tighter than the paragraphs around it. It was the part being read hardest and the part set tightest.

items.title: The agent can reach for a highlighter
items.text: Bold was the only emphasis it had, and bold was already naming terms, so nothing stood out. Now it can mark the few phrases your eye should land on first — in yellow, or in red when something is broken and green when something is confirmed.

items.title: A run of tool calls collapses again
items.text: Thinking models open an empty block before nearly every tool call. It draws nothing, and it was quietly breaking every group, so nineteen consecutive calls filled the pane one row at a time.

items.title: Recall reaches everything
items.text: Nine channels now — automations, insights, hypotheses and objectives join the five that were already searchable — with a filter for how much something matters.

items.title: Lab scripts are never stale
items.text: A custom script runs in its own short-lived process, so a shared library you just edited can't keep answering from a cache that outlived the edit.

items.title: Sleep counts what the work cost
items.text: A session is scored by weight rather than by its loudest signal, so token volume finally counts — and consolidation lands about three times on the busiest day instead of every half hour.

items.title: Upgrades can be seen through
items.text: Pending migrations no longer go blind when an upgrade moves the version past an unfinished step, so a vault mid-migration can still tell you what it is waiting for.

blocks.text: One thing worth knowing before you upgrade: verifying the migrations above turned up a defect where running install-skill first could silently skip them, permanently. That is fixed here, and guarded by a test that fails if anyone reopens it — but it is the reason to upgrade with dreamcontext update rather than around it.

closer.title: Upgrade, and let it move itself
closer.body: dreamcontext upgrade, then dreamcontext update in each project. The structural migrations run on that command, and anything that needs judgement is handed to your agent with instructions.
